documents.title: Developing course policies around A.I.
documents.stance_why: The CTT page says the faculty senate requires an AI statement in every syllabus but 'It is entirely up to the individual instructor to determine which policy to use', and it offers three example categories (permitted/encouraged, allowed under specific circumstances, prohibited). The document sets no stance of its own, so delegates with tiers listed.
documents.summary: The Center for Transformative Teaching explains that UNL's faculty senate requires an AI policy in every syllabus and leaves the content to instructors. It gives considerations for choosing a policy, advice on communication and citation, and example policy language in three categories plus mixed-use classes.

units.why: The page states the faculty senate rule that every syllabus must carry an AI policy, which is a requirement on instructors about communicating expectations (type P09 'Require an AI statement in every syllabus').
units.anchor: requires that you incorporate a policy related to AI use into your syllabus
units.policy: The faculty senate at UNL requires instructors to incorporate a policy related to AI use into their syllabus.
units.resolution_why: Coders disagreed on unit_stance (A neutral, B require). The source says the faculty senate 'now requires that you incorporate a policy related to AI use into your syllabus'. That requires instructors to publish a statement; it does not require AI use, so 'require' (AI use required) does not apply. Final neutral, with A's normalized policy, which repeats the source.

units.why: 'It is entirely up to the individual instructor to determine which policy to use' leaves the choice of AI rule to each instructor, so P04 (instructor sets the rule).
units.anchor: It is entirely up to the individual instructor to determine which policy to use

units.why: 'it is essential that you clearly explain to students what the expectations are' obliges instructors to communicate AI expectations, matching P09 (state expectations to students).
units.anchor: it is essential that you clearly explain to students what the expectations are around AI
units.resolution_why: Only coder A coded this. The source says 'it is essential that you clearly explain to students what the expectations are around AI use in your course', an instruction to instructors. Kept as a real policy statement; 'essential' supports must.

units.why: 'no one-size-fits-all approach' says the right AI rule differs by course, so decisions sit at the course level (P04).
units.anchor: There’s no one-size-fits-all approach here since courses differ vastly from one another
units.resolution_why: Only coder A coded this. The source says 'There's no one-size-fits-all approach here since courses differ vastly', the reason the choice is left to instructors. Kept as an informing statement under P04.

units.why: The page says there is 'a wide variation in AI policy across the university' (some allow any use, others prohibit entirely); this describes the instructor-by-instructor pattern, P04, as a fact.
units.anchor: Some instructors allow any use of AI in the completion of coursework, while others prohibit
units.resolution_why: Only coder B coded this. The source says 'There is a wide variation in AI policy across the university. Some instructors allow any use of AI ... while others prohibit it entirely.' It states the instructor-by-instructor pattern as fact (P04). Kept.

units.why: The warning that students 'may assume that the rules from their other courses also apply in yours' is the reason a course's AI policy must stay course-specific, so P11 (each course's policy governs only that course).
units.anchor: students may assume that the rules from their other courses also apply in yours

units.why: The page reports that the Student Code of Conduct now covers AI ('Cheating now includes taking work that someone else or an entity prepared'), which classifies unauthorized AI work as misconduct, P36.
units.anchor: AI has been integrated into the Student Code of Conduct
units.policy: The Student Code of Conduct's definition of cheating now includes taking work that someone else or an entity prepared and submitting it as one's own.
units.resolution_why: Coders differed on actor (A admin, B all) and anchor. The source says 'AI has been integrated into the Student Code of Conduct' and quotes the Code's cheating clause. The clause applies to the whole community and is reported here as a fact, so actor all. Kept A's anchor and normalized policy, which follow the source.

units.why: 'violations of your course AI policy should be treated the same as any other academic integrity violation' routes AI misuse into the ordinary misconduct process, P36.
units.anchor: violations of your course AI policy should be treated the same as any other

The source advises that 'violations of your course AI policy should be treated the same as any other academic integrity violation'. It routes misuse into the usual process and sets no limit on AI use itself, so neutral.

units.why: 'You should take time to talk about your policy when you discuss other elements of your syllabus' asks instructors to go over the AI rule with students rather than only list it, which fits P66 (explain and discuss).

That goes beyond listing a rule in the syllabus, so P66 (explain and discuss) fits and P09 (require a statement) does not. B's heading unit was merged into this one.

units.why: The suggestion to 'put an abbreviated version of your AI policy at the beginning of each assignment' puts the AI rule in assignment instructions, covered by P09 (syllabus or assignment instructions).

The source says generative AI 'is already being used in workplaces to speed up tasks' as context for the instructor's explanation; it is a fact about the world, not addressed to an office. Actor all. Both fit notes kept.

The rule is the instruction to explain the reasons to students (P66); the learning rationale is only the content of that explanation. Neutral because the unit sets no limit itself. B's separate 'Explain the why behind your policy' heading unit states the same rule and is not kept.

units.resolution_why: Only coder A coded this. The source says 'technologies are incorporating generative AI tools without always labeling them as such'. It is a fact about embedded AI, so P07 with informs. Actor changed from admin to all because no office is addressed.

units.why: 'it can be helpful to list specific tools when feasible' advises instructors who require citation or ban AI to name the embedded AI tools, which are often unlabeled, so the policy covers them; this is P07 and not P61 because the stated reason is that AI is built into other tools.

units.why: The example that 'using the Gemini tool in Google, CoPilot tool in Microsoft, or paid version of Grammarly ... counts as generative AI use even if they're not clearly labeled' defines scope for embedded AI, P07; it is a definition, so informs and general.

The source gives this as an example of what to mention: the tools 'count as generative AI use even if they're not clearly labeled as such'. It defines scope rather than commanding, so informs, and definitions are phase general. Kept A's normalized policy, which matches the source.

notes: Reconciled from coder A and coder B. Coder A. Example syllabus language on the CTT page is coded as units because it is the university teaching center's own sample policy text, with actor student. No school, computing or course documents were collected for this university. Only the two included CTT documents were coded. The three example-policy sections of the first page are model wording that instructors may adopt, coded as units of that page. Reconciler: no new types were proposed by either coder; the one UNCOVERED unit (AI risk varies by course) is left for the between-batch review. Example syllabus language on the CTT policy page is coded as units of that page, with the actor set to the party the example addresses.
